items.title: Arrival — settle in, then a yatai crawl
items.tldr: Land, subway into Hakata/Tenjin, and ease into the trip with a split-group yatai crawl once everyone's checked in.
items.pace: Light — arrival day. Subway from the airport, check-in, rest, then an evening out once everyone's ready.
items.body:
However the flight lands, the subway puts you in Hakata or Tenjin within 5–11 minutes for ≈¥260 — no need to rush anything else today.

For dinner, split into 2–3 smaller groups rather than trying to eat together: Fukuoka's yatai stalls seat roughly 8–10 people total, including other customers, and the city's own tourism board recommends parties of 2–3. Head for Nagahama or Tenjin, not Nakasu — locals describe Nakasu's stalls as the tour-group version, noticeably pricier and busier, while Tenjin and Nagahama are where residents actually go for a calmer night and (per locals) a cheaper bowl. Stalls open ≈18:00–19:00 and it's cash-only almost everywhere, so split the cash too. Regroup after for a nightcap wherever you land.

If the group would rather sit together than split up, Hakata Yatai Yokocho Kizuimaru (Daimyo, near Akasaka Station) is an indoor, all-weather mini-yatai space built for exactly this — see the Food & shopping tab for the booking details a party of 8 needs.
constraints: Yatai are weather- and owner-dependent — a stormy night can mean a stall simply doesn't open

items.title: Central Fukuoka — castle ruins, Kushida Shrine, Hakata ramen
items.tldr: A walkable loop through Fukuoka's own history and its most famous export, tonkotsu ramen, from the shop that started it.
items.pace: Balanced — a morning park walk, a ramen lunch, then shrine and shopping in the afternoon.
items.body:
Start at Fukuoka Castle Ruins (Maizuru Park) and the adjoining Ohori Park — free, and an easy ≈2 km loop around the pond if anyone wants the walk. October means no cherry blossoms, but the stone walls and foundations are there year-round.

For lunch, Hakata tonkotsu ramen at its source: Ichiran's Nakasu original shop (open 24 hours) or Ippudo's Daimyo original store, both walking distance from central Tenjin — worth doing once for the founding-shop, individual-booth experience. Worth knowing: locals themselves tend to skip Ichiran, viewing it as pricier "creative ramen" outside the three traditional Kyushu tonkotsu lineages — if anyone wants the shop residents actually default to, ask about Shin-Shin (Tenjin), known locally for a lighter broth (its own address/hours couldn't be pinned to an official source this pass, so it's a name to ask a local about rather than a mapped stop). Spend the afternoon at Kushida Shrine — its ornamental Hakata Gion Yamakasa float is on year-round display, free with the shrine grounds — then browse Nakasu for mentaiko at Fukuya, the shop credited with inventing it in 1949.

Dinner: motsunabe, Fukuoka's offal hot pot — order the champon-noodle "shime" to finish the broth. Motsunabe Kobayashi (Imaizumi, near Tenjin) runs the organizer's meal free with an all-you-can-drink course for parties of 8+ — book ahead (Japanese-only). Motsunabe Rakutenchi near Hakata Station is the walk-in fallback: no group discount, but its tatami seating genuinely holds a party of 8 without a reservation.

items.title: Dazaifu day trip — the shrine, the museum, the approach street
items.tldr: A half-hour out to Japan's shrine of scholarship, its national museum next door, and mochi on the walk between them.
items.pace: Balanced — one destination town, most of the day, back to Fukuoka for the evening.
items.body:
Take the direct Dazaifu Liner "Tabito" bus from Hakata (≈40 min, no transfer) rather than the train, which requires changing at Nishitetsu-Futsukaichi. Arrive as close to opening (≈6:30 AM in autumn) as the group can manage — Dazaifu Tenmangu gets genuinely crowded with tour groups by midday; locals independently confirm the same window, weekday mornings before ≈9–10 or after ≈16:00.

The shrine grounds are free; its Treasure Hall and history museum are small paid add-ons (¥500 / ¥200) if anyone wants them. Right next door, the Kyushu National Museum (¥700, closed Mondays — today works) covers Japan's early cultural exchange with the rest of Asia. Walk the Omotesando approach street between the two for umegae mochi, the local grilled-mochi specialty sold at shops the whole length of the street.

If the group has a few spare minutes, Komyozenji — a moss-garden temple literally next door to the shrine, noticeably calmer whenever it's open — is worth a peek. Treat it as a zero-commitment aside only: a maintained English travel reference currently describes it as not regularly open to the public, and several visitors have found the gate closed.

Return to Fukuoka by early evening — Dazaifu has little to do after dark, and it sets up tomorrow's earlier Itoshima start.
constraints: Kyushu National Museum is closed Mondays

items.title: Itoshima day trip — the coast
items.tldr: A car-or-taxi day on Kyushu's coast: a torii gate standing in the ocean, a waterfall, and trout for lunch.
items.pace: A longer day — Itoshima's sights are spread out and public transit there is sparse, so budget the whole day for fewer stops covered well.
items.body:
Itoshima's coastal sights aren't served by rail, and the connecting local buses run infrequently — for a group of 8 covering more than one stop, a taxi or rental car for the day is the realistic call over stitching together bus connections. Itoshima's own tourism association is explicit that local taxis are compact (max ≈4 passengers), so plan on two taxis moving together, not one — or look into an hourly sightseeing-taxi package, which can work out better for a group than metered point-to-point fares.

Anchor the day on Sakurai Futamigaura — the shrine torii gate standing offshore, Itoshima's signature shot, at its best near sunset — and Shiraito Falls, a 24m waterfall with an on-site restaurant serving yamame (mountain trout) set meals, a genuine regional specialty. Futamigaura's sunset view draws real crowds and a parking lot that fills fast, especially around the summer solstice and on weekend/holiday evenings; arrive at least an hour before sunset, or visit midday/on a weekday instead if the group would rather skip the crush. If the season's begun, Itoshima's oyster huts (grilled-oyster shacks, roughly October–April) are a strong option for lunch or an early dinner instead.

Check the forecast before committing to the full coastal loop — today's stops are outdoors with no researched indoor fallback nearby; a wet forecast is reason to swap this day with Wednesday's more indoor-friendly Dazaifu plan rather than push through the rain.

items.title: Nokonoshima's flowers, Hakata Okunchi, and the flight home
items.tldr: A ferry to a flower island in the morning, a free citywide festival if there's time, then the airport.
items.pace: Light and flexible — scale today entirely to your flight time; treat both stops as optional add-ons, not commitments.
items.body:
If the flight's in the afternoon or later, a morning ferry from Meinohama (¥230, 10 min) reaches Nokonoshima Island Park, whose cosmos flowers are typically in bloom this exact week — though the precise 2026 bloom status isn't published this far ahead, so treat it as likely rather than guaranteed.

Today also happens to be the first day of Hakata Okunchi, a free festival at Kushida Shrine (harvest market and free amazake 10:00–16:00, lantern lighting in the evening) — an easy add if it's on the way to the airport and there's time before check-in.

Pack the morning around whichever of these actually fits your flight, not both — this is a departure day first.
